title: Zenith Retail - Throughput & Failover Discovery
summary: Initial technical discovery about p95 latency targets, sustained token/sec throughput for streaming chat, and failover strategy between Hosted and Dedicated. Customer leaned toward Dedicated for predictable peaks but wants a hosted fallback. Agreed to run a two-week benchmark: steady-state + token-burst + multi-region failover tests. Next: send security pack, pricing spreadsheet, and bench run playbook.

Jon to share benchmark playbook and sample scripts for token/sec and streaming - due 2026-11-03
Priya to provide sample traffic trace and peak QPS windows - due 2026-11-06

header:
Date: 2026-11-01 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jon Park (Redwood SE), Tori Alvarez (Redwood CSM); Priya Nair (CTO - Zenith), Liam O'Connor (SRE), Hannah Brooks (PM), Arjun Patel (ML Eng)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we have about 45 minutes, we'll do intros, then Jon will go through the throughput and latency questions.
[00:12] Priya (CTO): Thanks, Maya. Quick background — we're building an in-store assistant that streams staff prompts and customer context, low latency matters at checkout. We're seeing spikes during promo windows, so p95 is critical.
[00:28] Jon (Redwood SE): Got it. What p95 targets are you trying to hit end-to-end? Is that token emission p95 or end-to-end UX p95?
[00:35] Hannah (PM): Good question — we care about perceived latency on the cashier terminal, so end-to-end customer visible p95 ideally under 250ms for single-turn responses up to 256 tokens.
[00:50] Liam (SRE): For streaming we also want stable token/sec during the stream; our telemetry expects at least 80 tokens/sec sustained per stream during busy periods but spikes to 200 token/sec for a few seconds.
[01:05] Jon (Redwood SE): Okay, that helps. Two axes — single-request p95 and streaming token/sec. For single-shot under 256 tokens, Hosted can usually meet 200-250ms p95 depending on model and region. Dedicated gives more predictable p95 under load.
[01:25] Priya (CTO): We also need automatic failover to Hosted if Dedicated capacity is exhausted — we can't degrade UX during promos. How mature is your fallback routing?
[01:33] Jon (Redwood SE): We have policy-based smart routing. You can configure hard and soft SLO thresholds, and fall back to a compatible model variant in another region or to Hosted with policy. There are trade-offs: model variant quantization can change output quality, so we recommend canary A/B tests for fallback.
[01:53] Arjun (ML Eng): How does KV cache behave with failover? If a session starts on Dedicated and then fails over to Hosted mid-stream, do we lose KV cache and is cold start latency heavy?
[02:05] Jon (Redwood SE): Good callout. We currently persist prefix/KV cache in a region-scoped cache. If you failover to Hosted in another region, you may have a cache miss; we mitigate with fast warmup and predictive caching for common prefixes. For strict consistency you'd want private deployment with shared cache, but that's heavier.
[02:25] Priya (CTO): Hmm. We're leaning Dedicated for primary, Hosted as a fallback — need numbers though. Can you show expected p95 delta under 50% concurrency?
[02:34] Jon (Redwood SE): I can give ballpark: for our medium-sized chat model (approx 7B quantized), Dedicated GPU pool in us-east usually shows p95 ~ 140-170ms single-shot at 1-3 concurrent streams per GPU; at 50% concurrency on your expected fleet you might see p95 creep to 220-280ms if not carefully batched. Hosted typical p95 for same model under national multi-tenant load is 180-260ms single-shot but more variance on peaks.
[03:06] Liam (SRE): When you say concurrency, do you mean concurrent active streams per GPU or multiplexed sessions? We multiplex a lot.
[03:12] Jon (Redwood SE): We're talking active token-generation contexts per replica, which maps to concurrent streams. Multiplexing and continuous batching reduces cost but can increase tail latency if batch windows grow. We have continuous batching heuristics to keep tail low.
[03:30] Hannah (PM): For our UX, we prefer low tail even if cost is a bit higher. We can provision Dedicated if the math works.
[03:38] Maya (Redwood AE): Noted. Priya, you mentioned peak promo windows — can you walk through expected QPS and burst profile?
[03:45] Priya (CTO): On a normal day it's about 120 rps across endpoints, but during promos it goes to 850 rps sustained for 6-8 minutes with short spikes up to 1.3k rps for 20-30 seconds. Roughly 60% of requests are streaming chat with context sizes around 512 tokens.
[04:06] Jon (Redwood SE): Those are helpful numbers. For capacity we usually model steady-state token/sec and burst headroom. Based on 60% streaming and 512-token contexts, we'll propose a pilot config that includes Dedicated pool sizing for sustained promo throughput and a Hosted failover slab for overflow.
[04:22] Liam (SRE): What's the expected token/sec per GPU for streaming with your runtime? We need to translate to number of GPUs.
[04:29] Jon (Redwood SE): It varies by model & quantization. For a 7B quantized variant on Ampere64-type GPUs, we see steady-state of ~1.6k-2.2k tokens/sec per GPU when optimized with KV caching and contiguous token generation; burst headroom can hit 3k tokens/sec briefly. Larger models drop this. We'll include model-specific profiling.
[04:51] Arjun (ML Eng): Do you bind GPU utilization to single tenant pools? We're concerned about noisy neighbor in hosted.
[04:58] Jon (Redwood SE): Dedicated is isolated, no noisy neighbor. Hosted is multi-tenant; we do aggressive QoS and preemptive routing but it's inherently noisier.
[05:06] Priya (CTO): Security — SOC2, KMS, audit logs. We may end up needing VPC private deployment for cardholder data.
[05:13] Maya (Redwood AE): We have SOC2 and can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for Dedicated and Private. Private gives in-region control and audit logs with longer retention. We'll share the security pack.
[05:25] Hannah (PM): Good. On the benchmark itself — can you propose synthetic workload scripts? We prefer to run a replay of our real traces if possible.
[05:32] Jon (Redwood SE): Absolutely. We'll provide a benchmark playbook with both: 1) synthetic token-burst tests to measure token/sec and p95 under controlled shapes, and 2) guidance to replay your telemetry traces to hit production-like patterns. We'll also provide example harnesses in python and k6.
[05:49] Liam (SRE): Network egress — we have strict peering; for Dedicated do you support private peering and VPC endpoints?
[05:56] Jon (Redwood SE): Yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering and private endpoints. For Private deployments we can do on-prem or in-customer VPC with full data plane control. Hosted requires egress but we can set up dedicated peering for throughput-sensitive flows.
[06:08] Priya (CTO): Cost — are there any burst credits or overage tiers? We don't want surprise bills during promos.
[06:16] Maya (Redwood AE): We offer reserved capacity contracts with burst options and an overage cap configurable per account. In the pilot we'll model a monthly commit and show cost sensitivity to promo frequency.
[06:26] Arjun (ML Eng): For streaming quality — if you quantize to save cost does that impact generation behavior for our prompts? We've had hallucination issues when switching model variants.
[06:36] Jon (Redwood SE): Quantization can nudge behavior; we do regression testing on your eval prompts and can pin model weights for dedicated pools. For fallback, we usually recommend a light-weight re-ranking step or a safety net prompt/temperature adjustment. We'll run an eval with your prompt set as part of the pilot.
[06:55] Hannah (PM): That sounds good. What about warm caches between bursts? If a promo starts cold, what's the cold start penalty?
[07:02] Jon (Redwood SE): Cold start depends on whether KV cache exists and model hotness. For Dedicated with pre-warmed pools we see cold p95 for first requests around 400-600ms but subsequent drops into the 150-250ms range. Hosted cold p95 can go higher on rare occasions. We can pre-warm with a predictive set of prefixes.
[07:20] Priya (CTO): Okay. Can you outline the pilot timeline? We need bench results before Black Friday prep.
[07:27] Maya (Redwood AE): Proposed pilot: week 1 - baseline profiling using your traces on Hosted; week 2 - Dedicated pool sizing and streaming benchmark including failover scenarios. We can aim to deliver results within two weeks: bench report by 2026-11-15.
[07:40] Liam (SRE): Are there specific telemetry hooks we should add? We currently export token-level timing but not per-segment KV misses.
[07:48] Jon (Redwood SE): We'll share a small instrumentation shim that emits KV-hit/miss and batch-latency metrics, plus examples for OpenTelemetry tags so you can correlate.
[07:58] Priya (CTO): Perfect. A few smaller Qs: do you support per-route SLOs and token-based quotas, and can we set model fallback sequences per route?
[08:07] Jon (Redwood SE): Yes to both. Per-route SLOs, quotas, and ordered fallback policies are supported. We'll map those to your traffic routes during the pilot.
[08:17] Hannah (PM): Any concerns with our 512-token average context and frequent system messages?
[08:23] Jon (Redwood SE): System messages increase memory but the runtime handles them; if system prompt is large and repeated, prefix caching is beneficial. We'll include recommendations in the playbook.
[08:34] Maya (Redwood AE): Quick recap and next steps — Jon will send the benchmark playbook and sample scripts, I'll send pricing and TCO, Priya to share traces, Liam to confirm peering windows. Target pilot kickoff 11/09 and bench report 11/15. Anything else?
[08:51] Priya (CTO): Please add a line item about a multi-region failover rehearsal — we want to test region switch and cache warming.
[08:59] Jon (Redwood SE): Will do — we'll include multi-region failover and cache-warm strategies, plus runbook.
[09:05] Maya (Redwood AE): Great. We'll follow up with calendar invites and links to the docs. Thanks all.
[09:10] Priya (CTO): Thanks, bye.
[09:12] (call end)

Notes on transcript: occasional misrecognitions (e.g., KV pronounced as "kay-vee" in transcript sometimes), some timestamps approximate, filler words removed in places but kept for authenticity. Shared artifacts mentioned: pricing spreadsheet (link: https://redwood-internal/example-pricing), security pack (link: https://redwood-internal/security-pack.pdf), benchmark playbook placeholder (link: https://redwood-internal/benchmark-playbook).
